proposedTopics.title: Proof-of-Stake basics
proposedTopics.description: Post-Merge Ethereum secures itself with validators whose activation minimum is 32 ETH. One proposer is pseudo-randomly selected for each 12-second slot, while committees attest and every active validator attests once per 32-slot epoch. Honest participation earns rewards; equivocation can be slashed and downtime is penalized. Economic stake, not hashpower, backs finality.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase01/pos-basics.md, explain validators, attestations, and finality in your own words with the 32-ETH activation minimum and slot/epoch timing. Done when: you can describe how a block gets attested and roughly when it finalizes.

requirements.purpose: Build a first mental model of validators, slots, epochs, attestations, and finality.

proposedTopics.title: Slashing & the beacon chain
proposedTopics.description: Ethereum's consensus layer coordinates validators. Slashing punishes provable equivocation — a double proposal, double vote, or surround vote — by burning stake and ejecting the validator. Ordinary downtime loses rewards and incurs offline penalties; the stronger inactivity leak activates when the chain has failed to finalize. This makes attacks financially self-punishing.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase01/slashing.md, list the three slashable conditions and contrast ordinary offline penalties with the inactivity leak. Done when: you can explain why running one validator key on two machines risks slashing.

requirements.purpose: Distinguish missed-duty penalties, the non-finality inactivity leak, and slashing consequences.

proposedTopics.title: Finality & fork choice (Gasper)
proposedTopics.description: Gasper combines Casper FFG (finality) with LMD-GHOST (fork choice). Fork choice picks the head by heaviest attestation weight each slot; FFG then justifies and finalizes checkpoints every epoch. Once finalized, reverting a block would require slashing at least one-third of all staked ETH.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase01/finality.md, explain the difference between a block being 'head', 'justified', and 'finalized', with the ~2-epoch timing. Done when: you can state the cost, in stake, of reverting a finalized block.

proposedTopics.title: Rollups: optimistic vs ZK
proposedTopics.description: Rollups execute transactions off-L1 and post data plus a state commitment back to Ethereum for security. Optimistic rollups assume validity and allow a fraud-proof challenge window, which commonly delays canonical-bridge withdrawals for days. ZK rollups post a validity proof verified on L1, avoiding that fraud-challenge window while still waiting for proof submission and L1 finality.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase01/rollups.md, make a table comparing optimistic vs ZK rollups on proof type, withdrawal latency, and trust assumptions. Done when: you can explain why an optimistic-rollup withdrawal takes ~7 days but a ZK one need not.

proposedTopics.title: Data availability & blobs (EIP-4844)
proposedTopics.description: EIP-4844 (proto-danksharding) added blob-carrying transactions: ~128 KiB data chunks committed to by a transaction, kept by Ethereum's consensus data-availability layer for a limited retention window, and priced in a separate blob-gas market. Rollups post data as blobs instead of permanent calldata, substantially reducing data-posting costs without bloating execution state forever.

proposedTopics.title: Sequencers & batchers
proposedTopics.description: Most rollups run a single sequencer that orders L2 transactions and gives fast soft-confirmations; a batcher then posts compressed transaction data to L1. A sequencer alone cannot authorize invalid state when the proof system and L1 contracts work, but it can censor or reorder, which is why L1 forced-inclusion escape hatches and sequencer decentralization matter.

proposedTopics.title: Account abstraction (ERC-4337)
proposedTopics.description: ERC-4337 brings smart-contract wallets without a consensus change: users sign UserOperations that bundlers collect, apply view/trace simulation to, and submit through handleOps(PackedUserOperation[]) to a supported versioned EntryPoint singleton. The EntryPoint validates and executes each operation against the user's wallet; an optional paymaster can sponsor gas. This unlocks social recovery, batching, and gasless UX.

proposedTopics.description: EIP-7702 (Pectra) lets an EOA authorize a persistent delegation indicator that points to deployed contract code, so the same address can gain smart-account features such as batching, sponsorship, and session keys. A later authorization can replace or clear the delegation; the EOA key retains ultimate control.

proposedTopics.title: Bundler economics
proposedTopics.description: A bundler is the ERC-4337 actor that pays transaction gas to submit a bundle of UserOperations and is reimbursed from each operation's prefund through the EntryPoint, including its fee. To avoid loss, bundlers simulate validation and reject operations that would revert or grief them, which is why the 4337 mempool enforces ERC-7562 validation and storage-access rules.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase01/bundler-economics.md, explain how a bundler is reimbursed and why it must simulate before including a UserOp. Done when: you can describe the griefing risk a bundler avoids by simulating.

proposedTopics.title: Paymasters & gas sponsorship
proposedTopics.description: A paymaster is a contract that agrees to pay a UserOperation's gas, enabling sponsored onboarding or ERC-20-denominated fees. Its EntryPoint deposit pays gas; a separate locked stake may be required when validation accesses shared state. The paymaster validates whom to sponsor, and weak replay, quota, or cost checks can drain its deposit.

proposedTopics.title: EIP-7251 & validator consolidation
proposedTopics.description: EIP-7251 (Pectra) raised the maximum effective balance to 2048 ETH for validators using compounding withdrawal credentials and added in-protocol consolidation, while preserving the 32-ETH activation minimum. Fewer validator indices can mean less attestation and aggregation overhead and simpler operations for large stakers.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What replaces mining under Proof-of-Stake, and how are validators kept honest?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Validators stake ETH and are pseudo-randomly chosen to propose/attest per 12s slot; correct attestations earn rewards, equivocation or downtime is slashed or penalized. Pitfall: security is economic — an attacker must risk stake, not buy hashpower.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How did the Merge change ETH issuance?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It removed PoW miner rewards, leaving only the much smaller PoS validator rewards (~90% issuance drop); with EIP-1559 burn, net issuance can be negative under demand. Pitfall: the Merge changed consensus and issuance, not gas fees or throughput.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What gets a validator slashed, versus merely penalized?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Slashing (stake burn + ejection) is for provable equivocation: a double proposal, double vote, or surround vote. Ordinary offline time loses rewards and incurs penalties; the stronger inactivity leak escalates only during prolonged failure to finalize. Pitfall: redundant setups sharing one key can double-sign and self-slash.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does 'finalized' mean under Gasper, and how does it differ from the current head?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Head = current heaviest-attested block (LMD-GHOST), reorg-able; finalized = a checkpoint justified in two consecutive epochs (Casper FFG), and reverting it burns ≥1/3 of stake. Pitfall: only data ~2 epochs old is finalized, not the latest block.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Optimistic vs ZK rollups — what is the core difference and its consequence?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Optimistic assumes transactions valid and relies on fraud proofs plus a challenge window (commonly ~7 days for canonical withdrawals); ZK posts a validity proof, so it needs no fraud window but still waits for proof submission and L1 finality. Pitfall: both inherit L1 security only if the required data is available.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is a blob (EIP-4844) and why did it cut L2 fees?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A ~128 KiB data chunk committed to by a transaction, priced in its own blob-gas market and retained only for a limited window (initially ~18 days) — enough for rollups to establish availability without permanent calldata prices. Pitfall: the EVM can access the commitment, not the blob data itself.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does L2Beat's Stage 0/1/2 framework measure?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Rollup maturity, not total security: Stage 0 meets baseline rollup/proof/DA criteria; Stage 1 adds a walkaway condition, a properly configured Security Council, and exit/challenge windows; Stage 2 requires permissionless proofs, long upgrade exits, and tightly limited emergency powers. Pitfall: criteria change, so use the framework changelog.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What powers does a rollup sequencer have, and what protects users from it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It orders L2 txs and gives fast pre-confirmations, and can censor or reorder (MEV), but cannot make invalid state settle when the proof system and L1 contracts work. Forced inclusion via L1 limits censorship. Pitfall: broader admin and proof-system risks still matter, and a down centralized sequencer halts the L2's fast path.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Trace an ERC-4337 UserOperation from signing to execution.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: User signs a UserOperation → bundler runs view/trace simulation → packs operations into PackedUserOperation[] and submits handleOps → the compatible versioned EntryPoint singleton validates the wallet and optional paymaster, then calls account execution. No consensus change. Pitfall: clients must target a supported EntryPoint version and deployment address.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does EIP-7702 change, and how does it differ from ERC-4337?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: 7702 lets an EOA persistently delegate code execution to a contract through a signed authorization, retaining the same address; the delegation can later be replaced or cleared. ERC-4337 defines a separate UserOperation/EntryPoint flow and can also serve delegated EOAs. Pitfall: malicious delegated code can control the account.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a bundler get paid, and why does it simulate UserOps first?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The EntryPoint reimburses the bundler's gas (+ margin) from each op's prefund; simulation ensures validation won't revert on-chain, which would make the bundler eat the gas. Pitfall: storage-access rules (ERC-7562) keep simulation predictive of real execution.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is a paymaster and what is its main risk?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: An ERC-4337 contract that funds a UserOperation's gas for sponsorship or token-denominated fees. Its EntryPoint deposit pays gas; a separate locked stake supports broader validation access. Risk: weak replay, eligibility, quota, or cost checks let attackers drain the deposit.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Name a headline change from Pectra and from Fusaka.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Pectra (May 2025): EIP-7702 EOA delegation and EIP-7251 validator consolidation. Fusaka (December 2025): PeerDAS (EIP-7594) plus blob-parameter-only scaling machinery. Pitfall: use post-activation upgrade pages, not pre-fork candidate lists.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What did the classic Ethereum roadmap tracks mean, and how is current work organized?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Classic taxonomy: Merge (PoS), Surge (scaling/DA), Scourge (MEV/censorship), Verge (resource-light verification), Purge (simplification), Splurge (miscellaneous). In 2026 EF Protocol work uses Scale, Improve UX, and Harden the L1, while ethereum.org tracks concrete forks. Pitfall: the classic tracks are not a release sequence or current org chart.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What did EIP-7251 (MaxEB) change and why does it help?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It lets compounding validators have up to 2048 ETH effective balance and adds in-protocol consolidation, reducing redundant validator indices and consensus messages; the 32-ETH activation minimum remains. Pitfall: a consolidated validator places more stake behind one signing setup.
